en: The Mahāvaipulya Sūtra King, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavat was staying in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove at Rājagṛha.

At that time, the World-Honored One was dwelling at the Bamboo Grove Kalandaka Monastery together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, as well as a multitude of great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
At that moment, King Bimbisāra of the kingdom of Magadha departed from the city of Rājagṛha and went to the Bamboo Grove Kalandaka Monastery to visit the World-Honored One.
He prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed King Bimbisāra, saying: "Great King!
It is like a person who, in a dream, sees a multitude of people and enjoys themselves together with various court ladies."
Once this person has awakened, they recall the multitude of people and court ladies from their dream.
Great King, what do you think?
"In such a dream, do those many people and court ladies exist in reality? King Bimbisāra replied, "No."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to the Great King,
“What do you think?”
Suppose this person sees a court lady in a dream and enjoys themselves together with various people.
Upon waking, they recall this experience—would such a person be considered wise?
The Great King replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
Why is this? World-Honored One!
In a dream, there ultimately exist neither a multitude of people nor a multitude of court ladies.
"If even the common people and their court ladies cannot be obtained, how much less could there be mutual enjoyment?
The Buddha told the Great King:

"Ordinary worldlings are just like this. When the eye sees beautiful forms, attachment arises; once attachment has arisen, desire is provoked; once desire is provoked, the karma of hatred and delusion arises—whether through bodily action, verbal action, or mental action."

The karma performed by that person, once performed, ceases; having ceased, it does not abide in the eastern direction, nor does it abide in the southern direction, nor does it abide in the western direction, nor does it abide in the northern direction; the same is true for the four intermediate directions, as well as above and below.
When the time of death arrives and the consciousness of formations is about to cease, that intention manifests before one.
Great King! Thus, regarding this consciousness of formations, one must inevitably experience the results of the karma one has created oneself.
"Great King!

It is like a person waking from a dream who no longer sees the court ladies or the various crowds. Once the consciousness of the final moment has ceased, the initial consciousness arises next; it may be born among the devas, or among humans, or in the hells, or as an animal, or as a hungry ghost."
"Great King!
Because the initial consciousness does not sever the continuity of one's own mind, one is born within that place where one is destined to receive retribution.
Great King!"
When one observes all that arises and ceases, is there even a single dharma that goes from this life to a future life?
Great King, when such formations and consciousness reach their end, it is called "cessation."
When initial consciousness first arises, it is called "birth.
Great King! When the consciousness of formations ceases, it departs without going anywhere.
When initial consciousness arises, it comes from nowhere.
Why is this? Because the nature of consciousness is detached [from any source].

"Great King! The formations of consciousness are empty of the formations of consciousness; at the time of cessation, the karma of cessation is empty. The initial consciousness is empty of the initial consciousness; at the time of arising, the karma of arising is empty. Yet, one observes that the fruits of all karmas are neither lost nor destroyed."
"Great King, you should know that it is through the continuous succession of the initial consciousness-mind that one experiences karmic retribution.
When the Sugata had finished speaking these words, he spoke in verse:
"All things are merely names; they abide only in conceptual discrimination.
Names are spoken through discrimination, yet what is spoken has no inherent existence.
By means of various names, various dharmas are explained."
Within the Dharma there is no such thing; this Dharma is the characteristic of all dharmas.
Names are empty of names, for names are devoid of names;
all dharmas are without names, yet they are explained by means of names.
This dharma is not truly existent, for it arises through conceptual construction;
that conceptual construction is likewise non-existent, and emptiness is taught by means of conceptual construction.
All ordinary beings say that the eye is able to see forms.
The world engages in false conceptualization, grasping at things as if they were real.
That which the Buddha has taught is seen through the gathering of various conditions;
this is the sequence of practice, for which the ultimate truth is explained.
"It is not with the eye that one sees forms; the mind does not perceive phenomena.
This is the primary truth, which is not realized by the world.

At that time, when the World-Honored One had finished speaking this sutra, King Bimbisāra of Magadha, along with all the devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others in the world, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly filled with joy.
The Mahāvaipulya Sūtra King Spoken by the Buddha.
